passages.t: An invitation to Ono, and an open letter
passages.happening:
The wall is almost finished, with no gap left, though the doors are not yet hung in the gates. Sanballat and Geshem send Nehemiah a message: “Come, let us meet together in one of the villages on the plain of Ono” (verse 2). ‘But they were planning to harm me’ (verse 2).

Nehemiah answers, “I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it to go down to you?” (verse 3). Four times they send the same message, and four times he gives the same reply.

The fifth time, Sanballat's servant comes with an unsealed letter. It says that the nations are hearing reports that Nehemiah and the Jews are plotting to revolt, that this is why they are building the wall, and that Nehemiah means to become their king. Soon, it warns, the king of Persia will hear of it. So he had better come and talk (verses 6-7).

Nehemiah replies, “There is nothing to these rumors you are spreading; you are inventing them in your own mind” (verse 8). They were all trying to frighten the builders, so that their hands would drop from the work. ‘But now, my God, strengthen my hands’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
If the workers could not be stopped, perhaps the leader could be removed, discredited or frightened into a mistake. The chapter shows three schemes, each aimed at Nehemiah himself.

The plain of Ono lay near the coast, near Lod, well to the northwest of Jerusalem, on the edge of Judah's land. A meeting there would have taken Nehemiah far from his people and into a place his enemies could control.

Letters in the Persian period were normally rolled or folded and sealed, so that only the person they were written to would read them. Sanballat's letter comes unsealed. It was meant to be read by the messenger and by anyone along the way. It spread the rumor while pretending only to report it.

The charge was dangerous. An earlier attempt to rebuild the walls had been stopped by the king on just such grounds. And it drew on real history: in Israel prophets had anointed kings, and Haggai and Zechariah had spoken hopefully of Zerubbabel, a son of David, a generation or two before.

The enemies' weapon is fear: they want the builders' hands to drop. Nehemiah's answer is a prayer for the opposite, that God would strengthen his hands.
passages.later: The charge of revolt had worked before. Officials had written to the king that Jerusalem was ‘that rebellious and wicked city’ (Ezra 4:12), and the work was stopped.
passages.asks: Nehemiah would not come down from the work God had given him. Ask what keeps calling you away from what you know you should be doing. And ask how you answer rumors about yourself: by chasing them, or by a plain denial and a prayer.

passages.happening:
Nehemiah goes to the house of a man named Shemaiah, who was shut in there. Shemaiah says, “Let us meet at the house of God inside the temple. Let us shut the temple doors because they are coming to kill you” (verse 10).

Nehemiah replies, “Should a man like me run away? Should one like me go into the temple to save his own life? I will not go!” (verse 11).

‘I realized that God had not sent him, but that he had uttered this prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him’ (verse 12). He had been hired to frighten Nehemiah into sinning, so that they could give him a bad name. Nehemiah prays, ‘O my God, remember Tobiah and Sanballat for what they have done, and also Noadiah the prophetess and the other prophets who tried to intimidate me’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Shemaiah's advice depended on the rules of the temple. The inner sanctuary was for priests alone, and the law warned outsiders not to come near it. King Uzziah had been struck with a skin disease for burning incense in the temple. For Nehemiah, a layman, to hide inside the temple building would have been both a sin and a public act of cowardice, and either would have destroyed his authority.

So Nehemiah tests the message by what God had already said. A word that urges a person to break God's law, and that happens to serve his enemies' plans, is not from God.

The mention of Noadiah the prophetess, and of other prophets, shows that there were several prophetic voices in Jerusalem at this time, and that some of them opposed Nehemiah.
passages.later: The law kept the sanctuary for the priests: ‘only you and your sons shall attend to your priesthood for everything concerning the altar and what is inside the veil’ (Numbers 18:7). And Chronicles tells how King Uzziah went into the temple to burn incense and was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16-21).
passages.hard:
How did Nehemiah know that God had not sent Shemaiah?

Shemaiah's words had the form of prophecy, but Nehemiah saw that they had been bought. The form of a message proves nothing; its source and its content must agree with what God has already said. Shemaiah's advice would have led Nehemiah to break God's law about the sanctuary and to abandon the work God had given him, and it served the plans of the men who were trying to stop it.

The chapter does not teach suspicion of every word spoken in God's name. It shows that a message spoken in God's name has to be tested, especially when it urges disobedience to God's law or serves someone's interests.
passages.asks: The advice came from a prophet, in God's name, and it was false. Ask how you test the voices that tell you what God wants. And ask whether any advice you have taken lately served someone else's purposes more than God's.

passages.t: Fifty-two days, and letters to Tobiah
passages.happening:
‘So the wall was completed in fifty-two days, on the twenty-fifth of Elul’ (verse 15). ‘When all our enemies heard about this, all the surrounding nations were afraid and disheartened, for they realized that this task had been accomplished by our God’ (verse 16).

Then a postscript. In those days the nobles of Judah sent many letters to Tobiah, and his letters came back. Many in Judah were bound to him by oath, because he had married into a leading family, and his son had married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah, one of the builders. The nobles kept telling Nehemiah about Tobiah's good deeds, and they passed Nehemiah's words back to him. ‘And Tobiah sent letters to intimidate me’ (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The twenty-fifth of Elul falls in the late summer or early autumn of 445 BC. Fifty-two days is fast. Much of the old foundation could be used again, the work was divided among many teams, and the circuit Nehemiah rebuilt was smaller than the city before the exile.

Even the enemies recognize ‘that this task had been accomplished by our God’ (verse 16). Human effort, planning and courage filled the fifty-two days, and yet the result is credited to God.

The postscript is a warning. The danger was not only outside. Some of Judah's own nobles were tied to Tobiah by marriage and oath, and they kept him informed. The word to complete in verse 15 is related to shalom, peace or wholeness. The breach in the wall is closed, but the breaches inside the community are not.
passages.later: The finished wall would be dedicated with two choirs singing on top of it: ‘At the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, the Levites were sought out from all their homes and brought to Jerusalem to celebrate the joyous dedication with thanksgiving and singing’ (Nehemiah 12:27). A psalm sings of the same God: ‘The LORD builds up Jerusalem; He gathers the exiles of Israel’ (Psalm 147:2).
passages.asks: The wall was finished, and the enemies saw God's hand in it. Ask where others might see God's hand in your work, and where they would see only yours. And ask whose loyalty is divided in your own circle, and whether yours is.
